proof_summary: Writing $N=2^K$ and $X=2^N$, totient bounds show that every admissible $m$ is at least $X+1$; moreover, $X+1$ is admissible exactly when it is prime, while $2X$ always has totient $X$. In the nonprime case, a hypothetical $m<2X$ must be odd and squarefree with $\phi(m)=X$; every prime divisor is then a distinct Fermat-form prime $1+2^{2^c}$, so multiplicativity forces distinct powers $2^c$ to sum to $N=2^K$, which is impossible because factoring out the least summand leaves an odd factor greater than $1$ dividing a power of two.
